clusters.name: Walter's move to Sorrel Valley, 1952–1953
clusters.reason: Around the family's move across the country in March 1952, within the year: your grandmother June grew homesick and wrote to her sister daily, then kept to her bed for weeks that first winter; your father Glen had fights at school and was sent home twice; your grandfather Walter stopped speaking to his brother Harlan over their father's land money and spent his days out in the trees away from June; the two rowed over money for new trees. By September 1953, June had joined the church choir and her letters thinned out, marking a shift in the family's settling.

clusters.name: Walter's orchard failed, 1968–1969
clusters.reason: Around the orchard's failure in May 1968, within the year: your grandfather Walter drank heavily most nights and rowed with your father Glen over who was to blame for the loan; your father took over the family's money and talks with the bank; your brother Carl's asthma attacks worsened that winter; you began wetting the bed again; your paternal grandmother Ida's heart trouble was found. By October 1969, Walter had stopped drinking and taken work pruning other men's trees, marking the family's shift.

clusters.name: Glen's job lost at the cannery, 1975–1976
clusters.reason: Around your father Glen's job loss in February 1975, over the year following: he sat in the truck in the yard for hours most of that year; he and your mother Marian had loud fights at night over money; your mother took a second job cleaning offices at night; you stopped eating properly and lost weight that summer, then kept to your room and said little to your mother; your grandfather Walter drank again after six years without it. By June 1976, you were eating again and made the track team, as your father started driving a delivery truck for the feed store.

clusters.name: Wilma moved into your house, 1990–1991
clusters.reason: Around your mother-in-law Wilma's move into your house in January 1990, within the year and into the next: you clashed with her over the children's bedtimes and meals; your partner Hollis worked late and kept out of the kitchen rows, then took his mother's side; your son Owen had tantrums at preschool; your daughter Lily came under Wilma's care; you developed eczema on both hands; you and Hollis rowed most nights. In June 1991, Wilma took a flat in town, and by August your eczema had cleared over the summer.
